provider_readback.text:
A trapped ant. A nylon snare. What did workers do when a colony-mate was stuck?

In controlled laboratory tests, Cataglyphis cursor workers dug sand, pulled limbs, and sometimes repeatedly bit the nylon thread restraining an active nestmate. Rescue behavior occurred in each of 9 group trials with active colony-mates, and in none of 45 group trials with other stimuli or controls. Each trial used five potential rescuers; only one to three workers actually helped in positive trials. These are group-level tests, not independent samples of 270 workers.

The restraint was artificial. The study did not show that every thread was cut or every ant escaped, prove empathy, establish the exact triggering cue, or measure rescue frequency in wild colonies.

Original primary study: Nowbahari, Scohier, Durand & Hollis (2009), PLOS ONE 4(8): e6573.
DOI: https://doi.org/10.1371/journal.pone.0006573
Full open-access article: https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC2719796/
Research evidence, limitations and credits: https://akshaymohan16.github.io/toxic-tales-library/sources/tt-009.html

Visuals: original schematic illustrations of ants, sand and nylon, not experimental video or measured individual trajectories. Whole-ant dorsal reference photograph of a related subspecies Cataglyphis cursor creticus (not the tested ant): April Nobile / AntWeb.org, CC BY 4.0, 960px Wikimedia Commons version, edited/cropped: https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Cataglyphis_cursor_creticus_casent0102116_dorsal_1.jpg
